terms.latin: rēs fictae, rērum fictārum f. pl.
evidence: Cic. Lael. 97: in rēbus fictīs et adumbrātīs (Lewis & Short, s.v. fingō)
Cic. Lael. 24: in rē fictā, opposed to in vērā (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The participle of fingere, “to make up”: what is invented, as against rēs vērae. As an adjective, fictus is “fictional, made up”, of a story as of anything else (Cic. Off. 3.39), and alone ficta are inventions (Cic. Off. 2.43). For a story as such, see story.

terms.gloss: a story, a tale; fiction, myth
terms.comment: Any story told (see story), and so a tale that is not history: Livy sets the poets’ tales against unspoilt records of what was done. In the plural, as a kind of writing, it does for “fiction”.

evidence: Cic. N.D. 2.5: opīniōnum commenta dēlet diēs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: From comminīscī, to think up: an invention, usually one passed off as true, so “a fiction” in the sense of a lie.
fābulōsus is classical, “legendary, fabulous” (Hor., Suet.; Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: incidī in māteriam vēram sed simillimam fictae
phrases.english: I’ve come upon a story that is true but very like fiction

phrases.latin: calumniārī sī quis autem voluerit, quod arborēs loquantur, nōn tantum ferae, fictīs jocārī nōs meminerit fābulīs
phrases.english: and if anyone wants to carp because trees talk, not only beasts, let him remember that we are playing in made-up tales
time wipes out the inventions of opinion

sources: Lewis & Short: fingo · Lewis & Short: fabula · Lewis & Short: comminiscor · Lewis & Short: fabulosus
Pliny and Phaedrus from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-plinius, loci-phaedrus); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 314.
